intro: Rachmaninoff plays his G minor Prelude: a clipped march with a generous singing middle. The march steals back almost inaudibly, then leaves on a quick upward sweep and a single high G.

sections.label: A · Short chords and marching bass
sections.mNote: Staccato chords punctuate the bass line

sections.label: B · A melody over broad arpeggios
sections.mNote: The left hand runs beneath a joined chordal tune

sections.label: Link · The march returns in whispers
sections.mNote: Ppp chords gradually quicken and grow

sections.label: A′ · Tempo I: the march restored
sections.mNote: Forte chords restore the march’s stride

sections.label: Coda · Upwards to a high G
sections.mNote: A light arpeggio carries the piano to its final note

cues.title: A march with gaps
cues.text: The piano marches in G minor, but its first steps are quiet. Short chords and rests punctuate a bass line that moves between them. Rachmaninoff marks the opening Alla marcia — in the manner of a march.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 20, bars 1–4: Alla marcia, piano, detached chords and rests. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2001
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The left hand opens out
cues.text: At Un poco meno mosso, the left hand stretches into broad arpeggios from a low D. The right hand joins its chords into a long melody. The piano suddenly has room to sing.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 22, bars 35–38: Un poco meno mosso; D-based arpeggios beneath the sustained right-hand melody. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2001
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The march under its breath
cues.text: The march’s little rhythm returns ppp, with D major chords above low octaves. The score asks for a gradual acceleration and crescendo. Its clipped steps become firmer as they approach the old speed.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 23, bars 50–57: ppp, followed by poco a poco accelerando e cresc. al Tempo I. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2001
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Back at marching speed
cues.text: Tempo I restores the original pace. C minor chords sound forte over the leaping bass, and the march keeps growing. Its short repeated notes now fill both hands.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 24, bars 58–60: Tempo I and forte; C–E♭–G chords over C octaves in the bass. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2001
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A very light exit
cues.text: The march dwindles. A G minor arpeggio sweeps upwards, marked pp leggiero — very quiet and light — and a short high G finishes the piece. Rachmaninoff lets the piano slip away.
cues.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 25, bars 84–86: pp leggiero, rising G minor arpeggios and a detached final G. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2001
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Low D opens the singing passage
transitions.from: A · Short chords and marching bass
transitions.to: B · A melody over broad arpeggios
transitions.how: The march diminishes to bare D octaves. At Un poco meno mosso, a low D begins a broad left-hand arpeggio through D–F♯–A–C, the dominant seventh of G minor. Above it, the right-hand chords join into a melody. The piano is marked pp.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 21–22, bars 33–35: diminishing D octaves and the new D dominant-seventh arpeggio. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2001

transitions.title: D major, almost inaudible
transitions.from: B · A melody over broad arpeggios
transitions.to: Link · The march returns in whispers
transitions.how: The running accompaniment slows and falls away. Low D octaves introduce a fragment of the march in D major, marked ppp. The same short rhythm continues through shifting chords as Rachmaninoff asks the piano to accelerate and grow towards Tempo I.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 23, bars 49–57: dim. e rit., ppp and poco a poco accelerando e cresc. al Tempo I. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2001

transitions.title: C minor at the old speed
transitions.from: Link · The march returns in whispers
transitions.to: A′ · Tempo I: the march restored
transitions.how: The accelerating march runs straight into Tempo I. Low C octaves support C minor chords, now forte, and a further crescendo follows. The piano keeps the same clipped rhythm across the join.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, pp. 23–24, bars 57–59: C minor at Tempo I, forte, followed by crescendo. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2001

transitions.title: The march climbs out of sight
transitions.from: A′ · Tempo I: the march restored
transitions.to: Coda · Upwards to a high G
transitions.how: The march’s chords descend and diminish. At pp leggiero, G minor arpeggios rise across the keyboard above the last low bass notes. A detached high G ends the piece.
transitions.evidence: Gutheil first edition, p. 25, final three systems: diminuendo, pp leggiero and the rising G minor arpeggios. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2001

composer.epithet: In exile he earned his living at the piano, while the bells of his Russian childhood kept sounding through the music he wrote.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen, newly graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 sat in the audience applauding. For a young composer, it was an excellent beginning.

His childhood had been less orderly. Born into a landowning family, he grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated; his sister Sofia died of diphtheria; schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the voices and bells that would stay with him. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a move to Moscow, under the formidable care of the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev.
